hints.hint: In "I don't know" puzzles, judge knowledge only from what one speaker holds. Fix that speaker's private value v and list every scenario consistent with v plus the public data, carrying any choice the problem leaves unstated, such as which quantity was published, inside the scenario, and allowing the two private values to be equal. Drop scenarios breaking the domain rules. One survivor means that speaker knows; two or more means they do not, so v pinning the partner under one unstated choice is never a contradiction. Key step: turn each announcement into an explicit predicate on that speaker's own value, list the values satisfying it, then enforce that same predicate on whichever slot that speaker occupies in every remaining scenario. Take announcements in order, re-listing between them, and answer with a coordinate of a scenario surviving all of them. If none survives, widen the unstated choices rather than boxing a plausible factor.

To locate all roots on one circle or line, find one necessary condition, not the n roots. From (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n take moduli of whole sides: |z-a|^n = |c||z-b|^n. Only then nth-root that scalar equation: |z-a| = k|z-b|, k^n = |c|; never apply the 1/n while nth powers still stand. k = 1 gives a line, their bisector. Else go straight to coordinates: z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 term, divide through by its coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius. Skip midpoint or diameter shortcuts; they invite sign errors. Radii are lengths, so a negative result just means a negative divisor: take its magnitude. That locus IS the answer; test one root at most. Report what is asked.

Union = summed areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Put the shared point at the origin with axes along the two edges meeting there; the cover is then the wedge x >= 0, y >= 0, membership is two sign tests, and far edges never matter. A corner at an interior point of S covers a positive-angle sector of S while its edge lines cross S, so overlap is strictly between 0 and area(S): reject every disjoint verdict and every containment verdict. Distance from a point to a side proves nothing, since the origin is a corner, not a center; skip tangency. Compute the overlap in the easiest orientation and keep that union as your working answer, replaceable only by another computed area. If the origin is a k-fold rotation center of S and the wedge angle is 2*pi/k, rotation permutes k congruent pieces, so overlap is constant and your value is optimal. State it and stop.

A maximum count is where an upper bound meets a matching construction; produce both. When each term may come from any of N functions, never compare adjacent terms: neighbours may use different functions, so no bound follows. Write the target at index n as explicit T(n); group indices by which function made them. On P's group, P - T vanishes and is not identically zero, since low-degree T cannot cancel P's leading term; so that group holds at most d = deg P indices. The cap is per group, so Bound = N x d, never N alone. For tightness, build rather than debate whether P can behave like T: give each function a block of d indices n_1..n_d and set P = T + c(x-n_1)...(x-n_d), c nonzero. P keeps full degree yet equals T across its block, killing the 'P must be low-degree' objection. Then answer.

Kill a fractional base first: log base 1/k equals minus log base k, so a point of height y has argument k^-y, and negative y means a LARGE argument. This sign drives the fit, the reduction, and every height, so settle it once. Fit parameters from the given points. A vector equality is ONE constraint; read the displacement off it directly. Carry one unknown: put a vertex at (t, f(t)), translate it, force the image onto the curve. A height gap d becomes one factor k^-d on the argument, giving a rational equation in t. First test a given vertex's x in it: the unknown vertex sitting there fits everything, so it MUST be a root. If not, a sign is wrong; refix, don't grind radicals. If so, divide it out; the wanted root is then linear. Take each new height from f. Area = |cross product| of adjacent edges.

Turn the requested event into a constraint on the sequence of moves, never into a symmetry claim: do not assume each item is equally likely to reach each position. Fix orientation once, since the earliest item placed on a pile stays at its bottom. Then see which steps the constraint forces and which are still genuine two-option choices; weight 1/2 per genuine choice and 1 per forced step, multiply along a sequence, and add the qualifying sequences.

For a huge indexed system asking for one entry, do not attack the full size: build a ladder of exact small analogues. Scale the toy faithfully -- if N unknowns meet conditions with exponents 1..N, use n unknowns with exponents 1..n and keep the nonzero right-hand side in the same relative position. A toy with more conditions than unknowns looks inconsistent; that is a scaling bug, not a contradiction, so rescale rather than abandon the method.
Solve n=2,3,4 exactly by elimination and record the target as a signed fraction. Fit a closed form in n, expecting factorial-type growth and a possibly alternating sign, not a guessed denominator. Re-substitute every n and confirm your candidate reproduces each toy value; an off-by-one in the factorial argument is the usual error. Then put in the real size and commit, instead of restarting a second derivation.

Let N be the unstated count of identical units, and recover it from integrality rather than from the story: if every per-unit share must be a whole number, N divides each listed total, so the admissible N are their common divisors and the intended one is the maximum feasible count, namely their gcd. When the story counts groups (streets, rows, batches), the units per group are also unknown, so write N = (number of groups) x (units per group) and solve for the second factor; a group count is never N by itself, even if every total happens to divide by it. Decide once whether each listed figure is a grand total or a per-unit amount, then stop revisiting it. Then add all component amounts, divide by N, and apply any markup or discount as one factor. Check each per-unit value is whole and answer the question asked.

If p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with p,q the same degree n, skip the degree-n^2 coefficient system. Seek a common fixed point r and use the centered form p(x)=r+A(x-r)^n, q(x)=r+B(x-r)^n. Composing forces AB^n=BA^n; factor once as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 and carry both branches, since B=A collapses to p=q; let the data, not a guessed sign, kill one. Inside the ansatz the identity then holds automatically - expect that, do not read it as underdetermination. Count free parameters against independent given conditions; matching counts force the answer. Combine those conditions symmetrically: two differing only in the sign of one part add to pin one unknown, subtract to pin the other. Verify p(r)=q(r)=r, then evaluate the asked inputs centered.

For "how many repeats restore the original" problems, simulate; don't theorize. Write the state as distinct labels and do each listed sub-step by rewriting the whole state: swapping two adjacent blocks concatenates them in the other order and leaves the rest fixed. Fix ONE convention (slot i now holds label X) and never mix in its inverse (label at i goes to slot j); that mix-up makes correct work look self-contradictory. After each sub-step check every label appears once. Never assume overlapping sub-steps compose to an involution or to disjoint swaps. Then repeat the full operation, counting until the state first returns to the original; cross-check against the lcm of the disjoint cycle lengths. Do the two smallest sizes exactly, propose a closed form, test it on one larger size, and if a size disagrees redo that simulation instead of patching the formula piecewise.
